seoTitle: DVT Workup: Wells Score, D-Dimer, Ultrasound and Treatment
metaDescription: The painful or swollen leg for EM and IM rotations: limb ischemia, necrotizing infection, Wells score, D-dimer and ultrasound, DVT doses, and cellulitis.
h1: The painful or swollen leg: DVT, ischemia and cellulitis, fork by fork
dek: For the student on an EM or IM rotation with a swollen or painful leg and a resident about to ask what is next: the limb and life threats first, the Wells score, D-dimer and ultrasound rules, DVT doses and duration, cellulitis and abscess antibiotics, and what you will be pimped on.

shortAnswer.text: Vitals, then both legs: pulses (handheld Doppler if impalpable), color, warmth, sensation, movement and the skin. A cold pulseless foot, a tense blue leg or pain out of proportion changes the route before DVT is scored.

shortAnswer.lead: Cold, pale, pulseless: heparin and a surgeon.
shortAnswer.text: IV unfractionated heparin on diagnosis unless contraindicated, and an emergency bedside viability assessment, with no imaging delay. Salvageable: revascularize. Insensate and paralyzed with no Doppler signals: amputation.
Emergency debridement within 6 hours of admission (WSES 2022; its 2018 consensus said 12) with broad antibiotics plus clindamycin or linezolid. Imaging and a low LRINEC score never delay it.

Two-level Wells: 1 point or less goes to a D-dimer (age-adjusted over 50), 2 or more to compression ultrasound within 4 hours. A negative D-dimer ends it; a positive one goes to ultrasound, never straight to treatment.

shortAnswer.lead: Apixaban or rivaroxaban, no heparin lead-in.
shortAnswer.text: Not pregnant, no active cancer: apixaban 10 mg twice daily for 7 days, then 5 mg twice daily; or rivaroxaban 15 mg twice daily with food for 21 days, then 20 mg daily. Dabigatran and edoxaban need 5 to 10 days of heparin first. At home for uncomplicated DVT.
Stop at 3 months after a transient factor that has passed; continue indefinitely after an unprovoked clot when the bleeding risk allows, reviewed at least yearly.

shortAnswer.lead: Pregnancy and cancer change the drug.
shortAnswer.text: Pregnant: compression ultrasound including the iliac veins, then LMWH, never warfarin or a DOAC. Active cancer: a DOAC, used carefully in GI cancers, or LMWH if a DOAC is unsuitable.
No MRSA risk: cephalexin 500 mg every 6 hours (NICE: flucloxacillin) for 5 days, IV cefazolin if unwell. MRSA risk: add TMP-SMX or doxycycline, or IV vancomycin if unwell. Pus: incision and drainage.

sections.heading: What do you check first in a painful or swollen leg?
sections.intro: The limb or life threat: acute limb ischemia judged at the bedside with a handheld Doppler, necrotizing infection from its clinical signs. Only then is DVT scored.

sections.heading: Ischemia, infection, DVT or both legs: which fork is this leg on?
sections.intro: Pulses, color and the skin pick the first route; then the Wells score, the D-dimer, the ultrasound, cancer and what provoked the clot steer the DVT branch.

sections.heading: How do you treat DVT, limb ischemia, necrotizing fasciitis and cellulitis?
sections.intro: Revascularize or amputate by viability, debride necrotizing infection now, a beta-lactam for cellulitis, a DOAC for most DVT and LMWH in pregnancy.

sections.heading: How do you use the Wells score for DVT?
sections.intro: Two-level Wells: 1 point each for nine findings, minus 2 when another diagnosis is at least as likely; 2 or more is DVT likely. Both legs swollen is a different workup: the drug list, NT-proBNP and urine protein.

sections.heading: Which ultrasound for suspected DVT, and when do you repeat it?
sections.intro: Compression ultrasound, proximal or whole leg, within 4 hours; the iliac veins included in pregnancy; a repeat in about a week when DVT is likely and the first scan is clear (NICE: if a D-dimer is positive); serial scans for a low-risk calf clot.

sections.heading: When does a D-dimer rule out DVT?
sections.intro: Only when DVT is unlikely on Wells: a negative result ends the workup and a positive one goes to ultrasound. Consider an age-adjusted cutoff over 50; it helps little in hospitalized, postsurgical or pregnant patients.

sections.heading: How long do you anticoagulate a DVT?
sections.intro: At least 3 months: stop then after a transient factor that has passed, and continue indefinitely after an unprovoked clot when the bleeding risk allows.

sections.heading: Where does each swollen leg end up?
sections.intro: Revascularization or amputation, the operating room, antibiotics with a marked edge, home on a DOAC, or DVT excluded with clear advice on when to come back.

checklist.heading: The swollen leg: what to check before you order a test

items.text: Pulses in both legs, with a handheld Doppler if they cannot be felt.
Color, warmth, sensation and movement of the foot.
Pain out of proportion, edema past the redness, bullae or crepitus.
Breathlessness, pleuritic pain, hypoxia or hemoptysis: the PE route.
One leg or both; pregnant or not.
Pus or fluctuance, and MRSA risk factors such as injection drug use.

rounds.present: Lead with the threats you excluded, then the score, the scan and the plan. For example: 62-year-old man 3 weeks after a left knee replacement, now walking, with a swollen, painful left leg; no ischemia, necrotizing signs or PE symptoms. Wells 4 (major surgery within 12 weeks, entire leg swollen, calf 4 cm larger, pitting edema of that leg only), so DVT likely, and compression ultrasound shows non-compressible left popliteal and femoral veins. No cancer, CrCl 78 mL/min, no bleeding history. Plan: apixaban 10 mg twice daily for 7 days, then 5 mg twice daily, at home since his pain is controlled by mouth and his wife is with him; provoked by surgery that has passed, so 3 months, then stop if uncomplicated, with written warning signs and a thrombosis contact; no thrombophilia testing.

pimp.q: Why not send a D-dimer on everyone?
pimp.a: It is for the patient in whom DVT is unlikely; a likely Wells score goes straight to ultrasound. It helps little in hospitalized, postsurgical or pregnant patients, in whom it is often positive, and a positive result alone never diagnoses DVT.

pimp.q: Why no heparin lead-in with apixaban or rivaroxaban?
pimp.a: Each starts at a higher dose instead: for 7 days with apixaban and 3 weeks with rivaroxaban. Dabigatran and edoxaban need 5 to 10 days of heparin first.

pimp.q: How long does skeletal muscle tolerate acute ischemia?
pimp.a: About 4 to 6 hours, which is why heparin goes in on diagnosis and imaging before treatment is usually unnecessary.

pimp.q: Why not revascularize a category III limb?
pimp.a: The damage is irreversible, and reperfusion of the ischemic metabolites can cause multiorgan failure and cardiovascular collapse. Revascularizing nonviable tissue is Class 3: Harm; amputation is the index procedure.

pimp.q: Why not TMP-SMX alone for cellulitis?
pimp.a: WSES 2022 says TMP-SMX and doxycycline have no activity against group A and B streptococci, so with an MRSA risk they go with a beta-lactam such as cephalexin.

pimp.q: What does a ruptured Baker cyst mimic, and what proves it?
pimp.a: DVT: synovial fluid leaks into the calf. The duplex excludes the clot, which is why it comes first, and anticoagulation without a DVT is the misdiagnosis to avoid.

traps.text: A D-dimer before the leg is scored. Wells first; the D-dimer only when DVT is unlikely.
Treating a positive D-dimer as DVT. It goes to ultrasound.
Discharging after one clear scan when DVT was likely. Repeat in about a week (NICE: if a D-dimer is positive).
CT angiography before heparin in acute limb ischemia. Heparin on diagnosis; imaging before treatment is usually unnecessary.
Waiting for gas on CT, a high LRINEC or 24 hours of antibiotics before operating on necrotizing infection. Debridement comes now; imaging and a low score never delay it.
Warfarin or a DOAC for DVT in pregnancy. LMWH, once or twice daily.
Anticoagulating a ruptured Baker cyst. The duplex showed no DVT.
An IVC filter in place of anticoagulation. Only when anticoagulation is contraindicated.

faq.q: How do you work up suspected DVT?
faq.a: Score it with the two-level Wells score. 1 point or less: a D-dimer, age-adjusted over 50; negative rules DVT out, positive goes to ultrasound. 2 points or more: compression ultrasound, proximal or whole leg, within 4 hours, with interim anticoagulation if the result will take longer. A likely score with a clear scan gets a repeat in about a week.

faq.q: What is the apixaban dose for DVT?
faq.a: 10 mg twice daily for 7 days, then 5 mg twice daily, with no heparin lead-in. Rivaroxaban is 15 mg twice daily with food for 21 days, then 20 mg once daily with food. Treat for at least 3 months. For extended treatment, the labels give a lower dose, apixaban 2.5 mg twice daily or rivaroxaban 10 mg daily, after at least 6 months.

faq.q: How long do you treat a provoked versus an unprovoked DVT?
faq.a: Provoked by a transient factor that has passed: 3 months, then stop if the course was uncomplicated. Unprovoked: indefinitely when the bleeding risk allows, reviewed at least yearly; NICE suggests discussing stopping if the HAS-BLED score is 4 or more and cannot be modified. No thrombophilia testing after a provoked DVT or while anticoagulation continues.

faq.q: Do you treat an isolated calf DVT?
faq.a: Not always. With mild symptoms and no risk factor for extension, CHEST suggests serial ultrasound over 2 weeks instead of anticoagulation, treating only if it extends; ESVS repeats a whole-leg scan at 1 week. Severe symptoms or a risk factor, such as cancer, a clot over 5 cm or more than one vein, mean the same anticoagulation as a proximal DVT.

faq.q: What antibiotic for cellulitis of the leg?
faq.a: Without pus or an MRSA risk: oral cephalexin 500 mg every 6 hours (NICE: flucloxacillin) for 5 days, longer if not resolved; IV cefazolin 2 g every 8 hours if systemically unwell. With an MRSA risk such as injection drug use: TMP-SMX or doxycycline added to cephalexin, or IV vancomycin or linezolid if unwell. Mark the edge; reassess at 2 to 3 days.

faq.q: How is acute limb ischemia managed?
faq.a: IV unfractionated heparin on diagnosis unless contraindicated, and an emergency bedside assessment of viability by a clinician who can revascularize, with a handheld Doppler; imaging first is usually unnecessary. Categories I to IIb are revascularized, by surgical embolectomy or catheter-directed lysis, watching for compartment syndrome. Category III, insensate and paralyzed with no Doppler signals, gets amputation.
